Yemen Financial Inclusion Evidence

The reform clock is moving faster than the people-side evidence

Evidence Readings/The reform clock is moving faster than the people-side evidence
Question

What can we say when regulations, projects and payment infrastructure change after the latest population measurement?

What the evidence supports

Several reform and infrastructure events have been recorded since the latest representative population-level inclusion survey, whose Yemen fieldwork ran from November 2022 to January 2023. The evidence therefore has to be read across several clocks: recent administrative change does not establish a population outcome, and the older population measure does not erase newer institutional change.

01

What supports this reading

Latest representative account-ownership measure available: The latest representative Findex measure available reports 11.9% account ownership for Yemen in the 2021 wave, with Yemen fieldwork conducted in 2022–23.

POS infrastructure expanded: POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) increased from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026.

The July 2026 Yemen SMP state is staff-level and conditional: On July 16, 2026, IMF staff and the Yemeni authorities announced staff-level agreement on key policies and reforms that could underpin a proposed 18-month SMP. The IMF stated that the agreement was subject to Management approval and would not result in Board discussion. It is not an IMF financing arrangement or an external-statistics crosswalk.

02

What qualifies or complicates the reading

Each stream has its own limits. The Findex measure covers adults aged 15 and over in the areas surveyed, which excluded about 23% of the population. The POS count is administrative, within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), and its monthly releases end in January 2026 on the CBY-Aden payments page as checked on 26 September 2026. The 2026 payment-institution records and the July 2026 IMF staff-level agreement, which was subject to IMF Management approval, are institutional states that measure neither use nor outcomes.

03

How this fits into the wider system

Yemen’s evidence is asynchronous. Administrative payment data and regulatory/institutional events can update quickly, while nationally representative demand-side measurement is expensive and episodic. Reading these streams together requires keeping them separately dated and asking whether the chain from reform or infrastructure to access, use, quality and outcome has actually been observed.

04

What the evidence does not establish

The evidence does not show whether inclusion improved or deteriorated after the latest people-side observation. Recent infrastructure, regulatory and programme events are not measures of people’s access, use, service quality or outcomes, and the older Findex observation is not a 2026 population rate.

05

Implication for decision use

Recent reforms and infrastructure can be reported at the state the evidence actually establishes. When a decision requires a population outcome, newer people-side measurement is needed; recent administrative events cannot substitute for a representative population measure, and an older survey should not freeze the description of institutional change.

06

What remains unknown

The current system cannot yet establish whether the recent infrastructure and institutional changes increased population-level access, use, quality or outcomes after the latest representative observation.

07

What evidence would change the reading

A new representative demand-side wave, aligned where possible to reform exposure and service-use questions, would test whether adoption followed infrastructure and institutional change.

08

Different dates: newer infrastructure and reforms, older evidence on people

Analytical text alternative
  1. Analytical question: How should newer reform and infrastructure evidence be read beside older population evidence?
  2. What the evidence shows: The latest representative measure of account ownership in Yemen is 11.9% of adults aged 15 and over, from the Global Findex 2021 wave (fieldwork 7 November 2022 to 9 January 2023; the survey excluded areas holding about 23% of the population). Payment-infrastructure data are newer: POS terminals reported within the reporting scope of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,473 in January 2026. Institutional and reform events are newer still, from the World Bank's approval of the Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) on 17 June 2025 to the first board meeting of the Yemeni Payments and Clearing Company (YPCC) on 4 August 2026. The evidence base holds no representative people-side measure after that fieldwork, so whether people's access, use or outcomes changed after these events is an open question; the difference in timing does not show that they improved.
  3. Scope and time: 2022–23 people fieldwork beside 2025–26 system events · Separate survey, administrative, institutional and programme universes
  4. What not to conclude: Newer infrastructure and reform events do not show current access, use or outcomes for people, and the 2022–23 survey value is not a 2026 rate.
2022–23 people fieldwork beside 2025–26 system eventsSeparate survey, administrative, institutional and programme universes
